catalog: Explore the fundamental AI algorithms used in simulations and game development. This course covers techniques like pathfinding, decision trees, behavior trees, finite state machines, and machine learning. Students will apply these algorithms to create more dynamic, responsive, and intelligent virtual environments. Ideal for those interested in game design, simulations, and AI programming.

goals.detail: AI algorithms such as pathfinding, decision trees, and behavior trees to create dynamic and responsive simulations.
the performance and effectiveness of different AI techniques in game and simulation environments.
intelligent behaviors for virtual environments by implementing AI-driven systems and solutions.
the use of machine learning algorithms in simulations, determining their suitability for specific scenarios.
a fully functional AI-drven simulation project that demonstrates the integration of multiple AI techniques.

assess.name: Quizzes
assess.description: A short in-class quiz each week on the prior week's reading and concepts.

assess.name: Progress Reports
assess.description: Weekly written update on project status: what was attempted, what works, what doesn't, what's next.

assess.name: Presentation 1: The Pitch
assess.description: Students pitch their simulation world: what living system or phenomenon they want to model, why it interests them, and what their agent will do in it.

assess.name: Presentation 2: The Agent
assess.description: Students demonstrate a working agent in their simulation world. The agent must perceive its environment, maintain some internal state, make decisions, and act. Code walkthrough required.

assess.name: Presentation 3: The Simulation
assess.description: Students demonstrate a running multi-agent simulation with at least two interacting agent types or populations. Emergent behavior, even if modest, should be visible and describable.

assess.name: Presentation 4: The Final Form
assess.description: Full simulation demonstration, code walkthrough, and oral exam. Students must describe what their simulation models, what emerges from it, what it cannot capture, and what they would do next.

sections.heading: What to Cover
items: What living system, phenomenon, or world do you want to simulate? Describe it concretely.
Why is it interesting to you? What about it makes you want to model it?
What will your simulation look like running? Describe the visual and behavioral outcome you are aiming for.
What is the central question your simulation will try to explore or illuminate?
What do you think will be the hardest thing to model faithfully?

sections.heading: Format
items: Spoken presentation — no slides required, though a sketch, diagram, or reference image is welcome.
You are presenting an idea, not working code. Depth of thinking matters more than technical detail at this stage.
Expect one or two follow-up questions about your concept.

sections.heading: What Makes It Strong
items: A simulation rooted in something real — a phenomenon from biology, ecology, physics, social systems, or game design — rather than an abstract exercise.
A clear sense of what 'interesting behavior' would look like if the simulation works.
Honest acknowledgment of what you do not yet know how to build.

sections.heading: What to Cover
items: Demonstrate a working agent in your simulation world.
Your agent must perceive its environment in some way — show this.
Your agent must maintain some internal state — show this.
Your agent must make decisions and act based on perception and state — show this.
Walk through the code that implements the agent. Explain the key methods and data structures.
What has changed since your Pitch? What did you discover by building?

sections.heading: Requirements
items: The agent must be running live in Godot during the presentation.
It does not need to be the final agent — but it must genuinely perceive, decide, and act.
Code walkthrough is required: show the GDScript source and explain it.

sections.heading: What Makes It Strong
items: An agent that does something visually recognizable — you can point at it and say 'see, it is avoiding that obstacle' or 'see, it is seeking the food source.'
Code that is organized and explainable. Spaghetti that sort-of works is less impressive than clean code that does one thing well.
Evidence that you understand the AI technique you implemented, not just that you copied code that runs.

sections.heading: What to Cover
items: Demonstrate a running multi-agent simulation with at least two interacting agent types or populations.
Show and describe any emergent behavior — even modest or partial emergence counts.
Explain how the agents interact with each other and with the environment.
What is working well? What is not yet working the way you intended?

sections.heading: On Emergence
items: Emergent behavior does not need to be spectacular. A flock that mostly coheres, a predator-prey population that oscillates slightly, ants that form a rough trail — these all count.
You should be able to point at the running simulation and describe what is happening at the agent level vs. what is happening at the population level.
If emergence is not yet visible, explain what you expect to happen and why it is not there yet.

sections.heading: What to Cover
items: Full demonstration of the completed simulation.
Explain what your simulation models — what real (or hypothetical) system does it represent?
Describe what emerges from your simulation. What behaviors or patterns arise that you did not directly program?
Discuss the limits of your model. What does it fail to capture? What simplifications did you make and why?
What would you do next, given more time?
Oral exam: the instructor will ask questions about your code, your AI techniques, and your design choices.

sections.heading: Format
items: Live simulation demo is required. Have a backup (video recording) in case of technical failure.
Code must be accessible during the presentation.
Prepare to discuss the AI techniques used (FSM, behavior trees, steering, etc.) and why you chose them.

sections.heading: What Makes It Strong
items: A simulation that does something genuinely interesting to watch — that makes you want to keep observing.
Clear, confident explanation of both the code and the phenomena it produces.
Thoughtful reflection on the gap between your model and the real thing — this is the most intellectually important part of the presentation.

sections.heading: Oral Exam
items: Questions may cover any AI technique used in the course, not only those in your project.
You may be asked to explain a specific node in your behavior tree, a transition in your FSM, or how your steering behavior is computed.
You may be asked 'what would happen if you changed X in your simulation?' Be prepared to reason about consequences, not just describe the current state.

progress_reports.description: Each week you will submit a short written update on your semester simulation project. These are low-stakes check-ins meant to keep you building and to surface problems early.
format: Approximately one paragraph — three to six sentences is typical.
Written in plain prose, not bullet points.
Submitted before the start of class on Tuesday.
prompts: What did you build or experiment with this week?
What is currently running and visible in Godot?
What did you attempt that did not work, and what do you think is causing it?
What is your plan for next week?
progress_reports.grading: Progress reports are graded on completion and honest engagement, not on volume of progress. A week where you spent three hours debugging one method and learned something is worth full credit. A report that describes no activity is not.

semester_project.description: Your semester project is a simulation you design and build in Godot using GDScript. It must model some living system, physical phenomenon, or artificial world populated by agents that perceive, decide, and act. The project runs through the entire course, from the initial pitch to the final demonstration.
requirements: Must contain at least two distinct, interacting agent types or populations.
Agents must use at least one AI technique covered in the course (FSM, behavior tree, steering behavior, pathfinding, etc.).
The simulation must run in real time and be observable — not just a console output.
Some emergent behavior must be describable, even if modest.
The project must be original work. Starter templates and Godot built-in demos must be clearly distinguished from your own code.
scope_guidance: Start with one agent type that works correctly before adding a second.
A simulation with two agent types, one emergent behavior, and clean code is more impressive than a simulation with five agent types that crashes.
Visual clarity matters — a viewer should be able to understand what is happening by watching for thirty seconds.
Your simulation models something real or hypothetical. You should be able to say what it is a model of.
ideas: Predator-prey ecosystem (wolves and rabbits, sharks and fish)
Ant colony foraging with pheromone trails
Flocking simulation (birds, fish, insects) with emergent collective behavior
Immune system response (pathogens and white blood cells)
Cellular automaton exploring pattern formation (Conway, Lenia, reaction-diffusion)
Social dynamics — opinion spread, disease propagation, cooperation vs. defection
